newsitem.title: USA: Clinton ponders line-item veto targets.
newsitem.headline: Clinton ponders line-item veto targets.

text.p: President Clinton's economic advisers have targeted a handful of items in the newly enacted tax bill that may fall victim to his line-item veto powers, the White House said Thursday.

Clinton, who this week signed signed a budget bill that aims to balance the budget by the year 2002 and a companion piece that cuts taxes by a net $95 billion over five years, has until midnight Monday to strike certain provisions from the measures.
He said during a news conference Wednesday that he expected to issue the line-item veto in reviewing the budget package -- mindful that such a move was certain to prompt an immediate court challenge.
"On line-item veto, our deliberations will continue through the weekend on that subject," White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said.
"We're down to just a small handful of things that are potential candidates for exercising a veto," McCurry said.
Asked if the list would have 10 items on it, he replied: "I'd say more one hand."
In the tax bill, 79 provisions were identified as possible targets of a veto. Other items also were singled out in the budget measure.
The small number of items that remain on the list compiled by Clinton's advisers means that most of the provisions identified as benefiting narrow constituencies will be acceptable to the president.

Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles, Budget Director Franklin Raines and economic adviser Gene Sperling met at the White House Thursday morning to "continue their analysis of some of the provisions," McCurry said.
Clinton was to meet with them later in the day for the first of a series of discussions on veto items. "I don't expect final decisions at the meeting," one administration official said.

McCurry declined to say when Clinton would act, other than "sometime before midnight Monday." Aides said privately Clinton might announce his decision Saturday, during his weekly radio address, or wait until Monday.

The White House spokesman said that because of the line-item veto, which went into affect in January but has yet to be used by Clinton, fewer special interest items were slipped into the budget package.
"One of the things we discovered in our analysis was that just the affect of the statute has limited the types of limited tax benefit items that are in the bill," McCurry said.
"So far ... our review shows that of those provisions, many of them are legitimate corrections for anomalies that are in the tax codes," McCurry said.
The law, passed last year, was touted as a way of reducing the deficit by stripping out special interest items in the budget.

Long sought by presidents and a key part of the Republican agenda when the party won control of both houses of Congress in 1994, the law empowers a president to cancel specific items involving appropriations, certain tax breaks and new or expanded entitlements.
Like other presidential vetoes, Congress can override the action by mustering a two-thirds majority in both the House and Senate.

The Supreme Court in June dismissed a challenge to the line-item veto filed by six members of Congress. The court however, did not rule on the merits of such a veto but said the six members who filed the case lacked the legal standing to bring the legal action.
Clinton said at his news conference on Wednesday that he was fully prepared for an immediate legal challenge once he uses the line item veto.
